HISTORY OF FLIGHTOn October 20, 2024, about 1951 central daylight time, a Robinson R44 helicopter, N881KE, was destroyed when it impacted a radio tower near Houston, Texas. The pilot and three passengers sustained fatal injuries. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 business/revenue sightseeing flight.
According to ADS-B data and air traffic control communications, the National Helicopter Solutions, LLC (NHS) commercial air tour helicopter departed Ellington Airport (EFD), Houston, Texas, about 1942, and flew north, then northwest toward downtown Houston (see figure 1). The pilot established communications with the Houston Hobby Airport (HOU) air traffic control tower (ATCT), Houston, Texas, local controller (LC) and requested the “downtown loop.” The LC identified the helicopter, approved the request, and issued the current altimeter setting. 
Several minutes later, the LC issued a traffic advisory for another NHS air tour helicopter, N233JD, that was at the pilot’s nine to ten o’clock position, two miles away, and northbound at 700 feet. The accident pilot reported observing the traffic on her ADS-B display but had not yet visually acquired the traffic and was searching for it. The controller instructed the accident pilot to maintain visual separation from the traffic, and the pilot was reading back the instructions when the radio transmission abruptly ended. No further communications from the accident helicopter were received. The air traffic control operations supervisor looked out the air traffic control tower window and witnessed the accident.
After the helicopter struck the radio tower, an explosion occurred and the helicopter fell to the ground. The radio tower collapsed onto the helicopter, and a postimpact fire destroyed the helicopter. The last ADS-B data point, captured at 1951:19, coincided with the approximate location of the radio tower.

Figure 1. Overview of the accident helicopter’s flight track.
Surveillance video, witness observations, and portions of the helicopter structure embedded in the radio tower were consistent with the helicopter impacting the tower about 100 ft from the top of the 1,003-ft-tall radio tower. Surveillance video showed the tower’s top and middle beacons flashing as the helicopter approached the tower (see figure 2); the tower’s lower beacons were not visible in the video.

Figure 2. Surveillance video image showing the accident helicopter approaching the radio tower. The tower’s top and middle flashing beacons are visible (NTSB annotation). PERSONNEL INFORMATIONThe pilot’s logbook contained an entry dated December 14, 2023, stating that she met the experience requirements of Special Federal Aviation Regulation (SFAR) 73, section 2(b)(ii)(A-D) for Robinson R44 helicopters.
According to company personnel, the pilot was hired in August 2024. A review of the pilot’s logbook showed the pilot’s first flight in a company helicopter occurred on September 23, 2024, and the last logbook entry was dated October 8, 2024. Investigators only obtained information about the pilot’s flight history with the company through interviews because, despite multiple requests, the company did not provide the pilot records that it reported were available. 
Another company pilot trained the accident pilot to conduct local air tour flights. The training consisted of traffic pattern maneuvers and autorotations. During air tour route training by the company pilot, the accident pilot flew the helicopter from the left front seat while the company pilot occupied the right front seat and provided tour narration to the passengers. The training included discussions of operating near high-rise buildings and a 700-ft-tall lighted pole near the Houston aquarium. The company did not have a documented training program, nor was it required to have one under 14 CFR Part 91 regulations.
The pilot’s husband reported that she had worked consecutively for about the last nine days before the accident. AIRCRAFT INFORMATIONThe current owners purchased NHS in December 2023. The company employed three pilots and two boarding assistants. The company’s principal base of operations was in Conroe, Texas, and NHS operated out of EFD and David Wayne Hooks Memorial Airport, Houston, Texas.
On October 7, 2024, the FAA issued a letter of authorization (LOA) “Commercial Air Tour Operations Authorization and Drug and Alcohol Testing Program Registration” to NHS to conduct commercial air tour operations under 14 CFR Part 91.147 with three authorized helicopters listed, including the accident helicopter. AIRPORT INFORMATIONThe current owners purchased NHS in December 2023. The company employed three pilots and two boarding assistants. The company’s principal base of operations was in Conroe, Texas, and NHS operated out of EFD and David Wayne Hooks Memorial Airport, Houston, Texas.
On October 7, 2024, the FAA issued a letter of authorization (LOA) “Commercial Air Tour Operations Authorization and Drug and Alcohol Testing Program Registration” to NHS to conduct commercial air tour operations under 14 CFR Part 91.147 with three authorized helicopters listed, including the accident helicopter. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATIONThe helicopter impacted terrain on the southeast corner of a level and open field, covered with a short layer of grass. The tower structure and support cables were found strewn on the field and on top of the helicopter (see figure 3). 

Figure 3. Accident site with collapsed radio tower.
The debris field extended about ¼ mile northwest of the radio tower and contained fragmented sections of plexiglass, main rotor blades, console components, upholstery, flight controls, and landing gear. Portions of the forward fuselage structure were found embedded in the radio tower structure about 100 ft from the top, consistent with the video and witness information.
The cockpit and fuselage cabin were fragmented and displayed thermal damage. Cockpit instruments and controls were destroyed. Cockpit and cabin door locking pins were found engaged in the locked position.
The outboard 1-ft sections of both main rotor blades were separated. One blade separated near the root and exhibited multiple separations along its span.
Portions of the flight control tubes were consumed by fire, and all flight control rod ends were attached to their respective flight control tubes. Flight control continuity was not established due to thermal and impact damage. The pilot’s collective was found in the full Up position, and the cyclic grip was separated from the cyclic cross tube.
The engine displayed thermal and impact damage on the cylinders and accessories. Borescope examination of the engine crankshaft, camshaft, connecting rods, and cylinders revealed no anomalies.
Postaccident examination of the helicopter wreckage revealed no mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation.
A Stratus 2s ADS-B receiver was recovered from the accident site and sent to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for data extraction. No data from the accident flight was found. A portion of data was recovered from a flight before the accident flight. ADDITIONAL INFORMATIONRadio Tower Information
The guyed tower, identified as TX 189B0-A, Federal Communications Commission number 1052552, constructed on June 1, 1987, was owned by SBA Communications, LLC, Boca Raton, Florida. SBA Communications purchased the tower on September 6, 2024. 
The tower was illustrated on both the Houston VFR Sectional and Houston Terminal Area aeronautical charts. Both charts identified the tower as an obstruction, 1,000 ft or higher above ground level (agl), and indicated that the tower height was 1,047 ft mean sea level (msl) and 1,011 ft agl.
According to a maintenance inspection report, dated August 5, 2024, the tower was 920 ft tall, and an overall height of 1,003 ft, including with the top appurtenance. Two sets of guy wires extended from the tower; the inner set extended about 100 ft, and the outer set extended about 340 ft. The tower was painted in alternating white and aviation orange colors. The report noted that all lighting inspection categories were checked and found acceptable.
The tower had flashing beacons at the 340 ft, 639 ft, and 1,000 ft positions from the surface. Multiple witness and surveillance videos showed that the top and intermediate beacons illuminated and flashed red in unison at a rate of about 30 times per minute. The lower beacon was not visible in the videos.
Four days before the accident, on October 16, 2024, at 2344, the following Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) was issued for the radio tower: !HOU 10/073 HOU OBST TOWER LGT (ASR 1052552) 294527.00N0952020.00W (7.4NM NNW HOU) 1033.8FT (999.0FT AGL) U/S 2410170444-2410312359.
According to the radio tower owner, the company issued a NOTAM due to the recent change in ownership while integrating the tower site into their Network Operations Center (NOC). An incident report showed that “all lights out” awaiting delivery to the NOC. The NOC used “all lights out” when a site was not communicating with the NOC and the NOC did not have the ability to electronically monitor the lighting. There were no known outages with the tower flashing beacons.
Previous Company Air Tour Flight Information
A review of ADS-B data showed that from October 17 to October 20, the accident helicopter (pilot unknown) conducted seven flights from EFD to the downtown Houston area, and back to EFD. All seven flight paths generally followed the same route (see figure 5). Five of the seven flights occurred after sunset or during the period encompassing sunset.

Figure 5. Google Earth image showing seven flights conducted from EFD between October 17 and 20, 2024. The accident flight is annotated.
14 CFR Part 91.147, Passenger-Carrying Flights for Compensation or Hire
According to Part 91.147, the operator may conduct nonstop passenger-carrying flights in an airplane, powered-lift, or rotorcraft for compensation or hire that begin and end at the same airport and are conducted within a 25-statute-mile radius of that airport. The operator must obtain an LOA from the FAA. Part 91 air tour operators are not subject to the requirements and oversight comparable to those applicable to Part 135 air tour operators, such as having a safety management system, and limitations and risk mitigations that can be imposed through operations specifications and operations manuals. Part 91.147 does not require operators to provide any pilot information on an LOA or perform checkrides; thus, the FAA therefore does not receive pilot qualification information through the LOA process.
NTSB Aviation Investigation Report – AAR-21/03
Based on a long history of concerns about the safety of various revenue passenger-carrying operations conducted under Part 91, on March 23, 2021, the NTSB adopted Aviation Investigation Report, AAR-21/03, “Enhance Safety of Revenue Passenger-Carrying Operations Conducted Under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91.” The report issued six new safety recommendations and four reiterated safety recommendations to the FAA. The report can be found in the public docket for this accident investigation. COMMUNICATIONSThe pilot contacted the HOU ATCT and requested the “downtown loop,” which was not a standard or published route but rather a general term used by some local helicopter pilots when requesting to operate in the downtown Houston area. The HOU ATCT LC identified the helicopter, approved the request, and issued the current HOU altimeter. 
According to certified ATC audio recordings, the LC issued traffic advisories to the pilot and another helicopter in the vicinity, consistent with FAA Order JO 7110.65, Air Traffic Control. However, the LC did not receive acknowledgment of visual acquisition from the accident pilot before instructing to maintain visual separation from the traffic, as required by FAA Order JO 7110.65. The LC did not issue a safety alert for the radio tower along the helicopter’s projected route of flight. A review of the FAA Falcon replay, which began about 30 seconds before the collision, showed the radio tower in line with the helicopter’s recorded flightpath (see figure 4).

Figure 4. FALCON replay image showing the helicopter’s flight track and the radio tower depicted by a large chevron symbol.
FAA Order 7110.65AA CHG 2, Air Traffic Control, in effect at the time of the accident, provides direction to controllers on duty priority and actions to take in response to potential hazards affecting aircraft. Paragraph 2-1-1, “ATC Service,” states in part:
a. The primary purpose of the ATC system is to prevent a collision involving aircraft operating in the system. 
b. In addition to its primary purpose, the ATC system also:
1. Provides a safe, orderly, and expeditious flow of air traffic.
2. Supports National Security and Homeland Defense mission.
c. The ATC system must provide certain additional services to the extend permitted. The provision of additional services is not optional on the part of the controller, but rather required when the work situation permits. It is recognized that the provision of these services may be precluded by various factors, including, but not limited to:
1. Volume of traffic.
2. Frequency congestion.
3. Quality of surveillance.
4. Controller workload.
5. Higher priority duties.
6. The physical inability to scan and detect situations in this category.
Paragraph 2-1-2, "Duty Priority," states in part:
a. Give first priority to separating aircraft and issuing safety alerts as required in this order. Good judgement must be used in prioritizing all other provisions of this order based on the requirements of the situation at hand.
REFERENCE – FAA Order JO 7110.65 Para 2-1-6, Safety Alert.
NOTE – Because there are many variables involved, it is virtually impossible to develop a standard list of duty priorities that would apply uniformly to every conceivable situation. Each set of circumstances must be evaluated on its own merit, and when more than one action is required, controllers must exercise their best judgement based on the facts and circumstances known to them. The action that is most critical from a safety standpoint is performed first.
Paragraph 2-1-6. “Safety Alert,” states in part:
Issue a safety alert to an aircraft if you are aware the aircraft is in a position/altitude that, in your judgement, places it in unsafe proximity to terrain, obstructions, or other aircraft. Once the pilot informs you action is being taken to resolve the situation, you may discontinue the issuance of further alerts. Do not assume that because someone else has responsibility for the aircraft that the unsafe situation has been observed and the safety alert issued; inform the appropriate controller.
NOTE –
1. The issuance of a safety alert is a first priority (see paragraph 2-1-2, Duty Priority) once the controller observes and recognizes a situation of unsafe aircraft proximity to terrain, obstacles, or other aircraft. Conditions, such as workload, traffic volume, the quality/limitations of the radar system, and the available lead time to react are factors in determining whether it is reasonable for the controller to observe and recognize such situations. While a controller cannot see immediately the development of every situation where a safety alert must be issued, the controller must remain vigilant for such situations and issue a safety alert when the situation is recognized. 
2. Recognition of situations of unsafe proximity may result from minimum safe altitude warnings (MSAW)/E-MSAW, automatic altitude readouts, Conflict/Mode C Intruder Alert, observations on a PAR scope, or pilot reports. 
3. Once the alert is issued, it is solely the pilot’s prerogative to determine what course of action, if any, will be taken.
a. Terrain/Obstruction Alert. Immediately issue/initiate an alert to an aircraft if you are aware the aircraft is at an altitude that, in your judgement, places it in unsafe proximity to terrain and/or obstructions. Issue the alert as follows:
PHRASEOLOGY – 
LOW ALTITUDE ALERT (call sign), 
CHECK YOUR ALTITUDE IMMEDIATELY.
Paragraph 7-6-1. “Application” states in part:
a. Basic radar services for visual flight rules (VFR) aircraft must include”
1. Safety alerts.
2. Traffic advisories
3. Limited radar vectoring when requested by the pilot.
4. Sequencing at locations where procedures have been established for this purpose and/or when covered by a LOA.

The accident pilot had requested to transition through Class B airspace but had not requested MSAW services.

A VFR aircraft is required to request altitude alerts specifically. The controller would make a keyboard entry that would turn on the MSAW processing on the control tower radar display. MSAW alerts are disabled on VFR aircraft by default, because it can generate nuisance alerts, especially with helicopters flying low altitude routes. This would not preclude the issuance of safety alerts, which are required if the controller is aware that a situation exists that in their judgment places the aircraft in unsafe proximity to terrain or obstructions. VFR pilots remain responsible for maintaining clearance from terrain and obstructions while receiving ATC services.

An FAA safety review team found that the air traffic manager (ATM) described the traffic volume as light with routine complexity and that there were no unusual factors that would cause a distraction. The HOU ATCT personnel included four certified professional controllers (CPCs), two trainees, and one operations supervisor. At the time of the accident, two CPCs and one trainee were available, and the operations supervisor was providing direct supervision. The position configuration was normal for the time of day and volume of traffic. MEDICAL AND PATHOLOGICAL INFORMATIONAn autopsy of the pilot was performed by the Harris County Institute of Forensic Science, Houston, Texas. The cause of death was multiple blunt force injuries.
The FAA Forensic Sciences Laboratory performed toxicological testing of specimens from the pilot. Testing detected glucose at 17 mg/dL in the pilot’s urine; no drugs or ethanol were detected.

20241021195350.fa:
On October 20, 2024, about 1600 eastern daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Lancair 360, N510G, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident in Cross City, Florida. The commercial pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.

The pilot had filed an instrument flight rules flight plan from Atmore Municipal Airport (0R1), Atmore, Alabama to Cross City Airport (CTY), Cross City, Florida. The pilot reported in his flight plan an estimated time enroute time of 2 hours, and that there were 4 hours of fuel aboard the airplane.
 
Review of preliminary Federal Aviation Administration Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) data revealed that the airplane departed 0R1 about 1430. At 1520, while in contact with Tallahassee approach control, the airplane’s ADS-B track and radio contact with the pilot were lost. The air traffic controllers made multiple attempts to re-establish communication including identifying turns, instructions to “squawk IDENT,” and transmitting on the VHF emergency frequency, with no response from the accident airplane. 

As the airplane left the Tallahassee approach control area it was handed off to Jacksonville Air Route Traffic Control Center (ARTCC), who also attempted to contact the pilot with no response. Jacksonville ARTCC continued to track the airplane as a primary radar target until radar contact was lost about 24 miles from CTY. Another pilot, who was flying into CTY about the time of the accident, reported that he heard the accident airplane make a radio transmission on the CTY common traffic advisory frequency. The accident pilot stated there had been an electrical failure, that he was transmitting with a handheld radio, and that he was requesting a “gear check” while on the downwind leg of the traffic pattern for runway 4. After hearing no response from anyone on the ground, the other pilot reported that he offered to check the accident airplane’s landing gear, but he received no response. A short time later he heard an emergency locator transmitter broadcasting on the VHF emergency frequency and saw debris as he overflew CTY. 

A witness, who lived near CTY and heard the airplane as it flew overhead, described that the engine sounded like it was “spitting, sputtering, and backfiring through the exhaust.” An eyewitness on the ground reported that the airplane overflew the fixed base operator building at CTY at an altitude of about 600 to 700 ft. He described that the airplane’s engine sounded like it was “missing.” He added that as the airplane overflew the airport, it began a left descending turn. About 100 ft above the ground, the left wing and nose of the airplane dropped suddenly, and the airplane impacted the ground. 

The airplane came to rest on the airport property, about 4,500 ft from the runway 4 threshold, and 210 ft right of the runway 4 centerline, between runway 4 and taxiway Bravo. The debris path was about 160 ft in length and was oriented on a magnetic heading of 048°. All major components of the airplane were discovered along the debris path. The initial ground impact scar was about 100 ft from the main wreckage site and green lens glass was observed in the scar. The main wreckage was oriented on a magnetic heading of 340°. The outboard section of the right wing was observed about 60 ft past the main wreckage and was the last piece of debris observed.

Control continuity was confirmed from the left aileron, elevator, and rudder flight control surfaces to the flight controls in the cockpit. The right aileron remained attached to the right wing section, which was impact-separated from the fuselage. Control continuity of the right aileron could not be confirmed due to impact damage. The flap drive motor and worm gear were not extended, which corresponded to the flaps being in an “up” position. The landing gear position selector was found in the “retract” position. Fuel was found throughout the airframe fuel system, in both wing fuel tank boost pumps and filters, in the header tank boost pump and filter, and in the fuel strainer. The header fuel tank and both wing fuel tanks were breached during the impact sequence, and each contained no residual fuel. No evidence of fuel smell or vegetation blight was observed at the accident site.

The airplane was equipped with two engine-driven alternators. One belt-driven alternator was installed to the front of the engine, and remained attached. The drive belt for the alternator remained attached to the alternator pully and was intact. The second alternator was installed on the engine’s accessory case and was directly driven from the engine’s accessory section. The main 12-volt battery remained attached to the fuselage, and when measured with a multimeter, about 11.8 volts were observed. A second 12-volt battery was impact separated and found in the wreckage debris path. When measured with a multimeter, about 12.5 volts were observed.

The engine remained partially attached to the fuselage through the tubular mount and was upside down at the accident site. Thumb compression and suction were confirmed during postaccident examination of the engine. Crankshaft and valvetrain continuity were confirmed through multiple rotations of the crankshaft. The engine was equipped with two E-Mag electronic ignition systems. Oil was present in the oil sump and the oil filter was impact-separated from the engine. Fuel was observed in the engine-driven fuel pump, fuel servo, and the fuel flow divider.

A fuel receipt was discovered in the wreckage indicating the pilot had purchased 15.69 gallons of 100LL aviation fuel the morning of October 20 at Jasper County Airport – Bell Field (JAS), Jasper, Texas. Another receipt from 0R1 showed that the pilot had purchased 24.13 gallons of 100LL aviation fuel at 1313. 

The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.

The pilot reported that during a go-around after a bounced landing, the engine did not produce full power. The pilot chose to perform the go-around due to the bounced landing on the short, grass runway. During engine throttle application, the pilot noticed that the airplane did not attain the normal acceleration rate. The pilot verified the position of the cockpit engine controls; however, the airplane was still underperforming. Before the pilot could attempt any further actions, the airplane settled into the tree line at the end of the runway, impacted multiple trees, and came to rest inverted about 4 feet off the ground, which resulted in substantial damage to both wings, the fuselage, and the empennage. Multiple witnesses reported that the engine sounded as if it was not producing full rated power. 
Postaccident examination of the airframe revealed no evidence of mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation. However, a review of recorded engine data showed that the engine was not producing full power during the approach, landing, and go-around. 
Recorded engine monitor data indicated a sharp drop in the No. 1 cylinder’s Exhaust Gas Temperature (EGT) from 1321° F to 365° F as the pilot was turning onto final approach. Over the next minute, the No. 1 cylinder’s EGT rebounded twice before again falling relative to the other cylinders’ EGTs. When the pilot applied full engine power during the go-around, the No. 1 cylinder’s EGT jumped from 532° F to 863° F for less than one second before again dropping down to 526° F. Three seconds later the No. 1 cylinder’s EGT returned to normal, in line with the other cylinders; however, full engine power was not restored until 11 seconds after the pilot commanded full engine power. This is likely the No. 1 cylinder air fuel mixture was too lean for proper combustion. 
At the start of the initial decent, the highest recorded cylinder EGT temperature was 1,467° F and the lowest 1,306° F. At the start of the descent from traffic pattern altitude for landing, the highest recorded cylinder EGT was 1,480° and the lowest was 1,351° F. During the go-around, the fuel flow was steady at about 10 gph until the end of the recording when the fuel flow suddenly increased to 15 gph in about one second.
Additional review of the engine data revealed that during takeoff and initial climb, the maximum recorded fuel flow was 20.6 gph which is 2.4 gallons below the minimum required full engine power fuel flow of 23.0 gph. Review of the maintenance logbooks did not reveal a fuel injection system calibration during the most recent annual inspection as required by manufacturer’s maintenance manual. Due to a lack of recent calibration of the fuel injector system, it is likely that the system would not have provided the required fuel flow to the engine. 
On the accident flight, the pilot likely did not enrichen the mixture before starting the descent until after established in the go-around. During the go-around, the pilot likely observed that the mixture was not properly set when he noticed the degraded performance of the engine. This is consistent with the sudden increase in recorded fuel flow and engine power before end of the data and subsequent impact with trees.
20241021195354.fa:
On October 17, 2024, about 1432 central daylight time, a Mooney M20K airplane, N231MW, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Elizabeth, Louisiana. The pilot and passenger were uninjured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot reported that during a go-around after a bounced landing at WC Field (LS46) in Elizabeth, Louisiana, the engine did not produce full power. The pilot chose to perform the go-around due to the bounced landing on the short, grass runway. During engine throttle application, the pilot noticed that the airplane did not attain the normal acceleration rate. The pilot verified the position of the cockpit engine controls; however, the airplane was still underperforming. Before the pilot could attempt any further actions, the airplane settled into the tree line at the departure end of the runway, impacted multiple trees, and came to rest inverted about four feet off the ground, resulting in substantial damage to both wings, the fuselage, and the empennage. Multiple witnesses reported that the engine sounded as if it was not producing full rated power. 
Postaccident examination of the airframe revealed no evidence of mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation. The engine had continuity from the crankshaft to the accessory section and the valves operated normally when the engine was rotated by hand with the propeller. A borescope inspection of the cylinders did not reveal any abnormalities.
The airplane was equipped with an Electronics International MVP-50P digital engine monitor, which was recovered and successfully downloaded by the NTSB Vehicle Records Laboratory. Review of the engine data indicated that the engine fuel flow and the No. 1 cylinder’s EGT varied considerably during the approach, landing, and go-around (see figure). 

Figure. Plot of engine parameters for about the final 3 minutes of the accident flight.
According to the engine manufacturer, the recorded engine data shows that the No. 1 cylinder operates with the leanest fuel air mixture. As the pilot was turning onto final approach for runway 18, the engine monitor recorded a decrease in the No. 1 cylinder EGT from 1321° F to 365° F. Over the next minute, the No. 1 cylinder EGT increased twice before decreasing relative to the other cylinder EGTs. At 1432:26, when the pilot applied full engine power during the go-around, the No. 1 cylinder EGT increased from 532° F to 863° F for less than one second before decreasing back to 526° F. Three seconds later, the No. cylinder 1 EGT again began to positively correlate with the other cylinders’ EGTs. However, full engine power was not regained for about 11 seconds after the pilot applied full engine power. 
At 1413:24, at the start of the initial decent from cruise altitude, the highest recorded cylinder EGT temperature was 1467° F and the lowest 1306° F. At the start of the descent from traffic pattern altitude for landing, the highest recorded cylinder EGT was still about the same at 1480° and the coldest at 1351° F. 
During the go-around, the fuel flow was steady at about 10 gph until the end of the recording when the fuel flow suddenly increased to 15 gph in about one second.
Additional review of the engine data revealed that during takeoff and initial climb, the maximum recorded fuel flow was 20.6 gph, which is 2.4 gallons below the minimum required full engine power fuel flow of 23.0 gph. 
Review of the maintenance logbooks did not reveal a fuel injection system calibration during the most recent annual inspection. This system calibration is required by Continental to be performed annually by 6-4.7 in Chapter 6 of the M-0 Standard Practice Maintenance Manual. According to the engine manufacture, the lack of calibration of the fuel injector system would prevent the engine from receiving the required fuel flow.

20241021195360.an:
The pilot reported that while performing a touch and go landing to a private turf strip and due to forward visibility limitations in the airplane, he was in a slip during approach with the left rudder applied and the right wing in a low attitude. The wind was from the southwest at 8 to 10 knots, and he maneuvered the airplane to land to the north. The pilot stated that during the touchdown, the airplane pulled to the left, and the left wing contacted tall grass on the left side of the runway, which pulled the airplane further to the left. The pilot then lost airplane control and was unable to remain on the turf strip. The airplane came to rest upright in the grass. The airplane sustained substantial damage to both wings. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures that contributed to the accident, but thought the brake might have locked up during the landing. The reported brake issue could not be substantiated, and further information could not be obtained from the pilot.
The pilot did not possess a rating for single-engine land airplanes but had flown 2,159 hours in single-engine airplanes and 174 hours in the accident airplane make and model. The pilot’s most recent flight review was about 5 years prior to the accident.

20241028195380.an:
The pilot reported that he performed a flight control check before departing in his experimental, amateur-built airplane, and that the flight controls operated normally. During the initial climb, about 30 to 50 ft above ground level, the elevator control went slack. He could not regain elevator control and adjusted engine power in an attempt to regain control of the airplane’s pitch; however, the airplane descended and impacted the runway surface. The airplane skidded off the runway, the pilot egressed, and the airplane was destroyed by postimpact fire.
A postaccident examination of the airplane found that the top elevator control cable was not attached to the elevator horn. The securing bolt, nut, and cotter pin were not located. The lower elevator control cable remained attached via its bolt, but the securing nut and cotter pin were not located. A review of maintenance information about the airplane revealed that the airplane was originally assembled about three years before the accident, and had undergone several condition inspections, including one by a mechanic who was different than the owner/builder. The most recent condition inspection was performed by the owner/builder about nine months before the accident, and would have included inspection of all flight control surfaces. There was no logbook record of any recent maintenance to the elevator, nor did the pilot recall any. Based on the available information, it is likely that the elevator control cable was improperly secured during maintenance; however, when the maintenance occurred could not be determined.

After the airplane was originally assembled in 2021, it was inspected by a Federal Aviation Administration Designated Airworthiness Representative, who would have checked the build.
